visuals.heading: What a Product Designer Actually Owns

items.text: It is a good career with a bad front door.
The word "product designer" now covers five layers of work.
A salary is a tool to save and learn.
Who pays: founders and small teams that need a designer for a defined job.
How they trust you: a live project they can open, a referral, and a clear first call.
Before you commit money or years, pass the three proofs: Show it, Say it and Proof of Value.
Ship one real thing for a real person: a live site for a local business, or a tested prototype for a small product.
Walk a stranger through the project in two minutes: the problem, your choice, the trade-off, the result.

blocks.heading: Is Product Design
blocks.sourceSectionTitle: What a product designer actually owns

rows: 1. Discovery
Talking to customers, reading support tickets, watching recordings, writing down the real problem in one sentence.
A one-page problem brief backed by 5 to 8 real conversations.
2. Interaction
Flows, wireframes, states (empty, error, loading), prototypes that people can click and break.
A clickable prototype plus notes on what failed when real people tried it.
3. Visual
Type, spacing, colour, icons, motion. Making a tested structure feel trustworthy.
Before and after screens with the reason for each change.
4. System
Components, tokens, naming, documentation so ten designers and a dozen engineers build the same thing.
A small, documented component library used in a real project.
5. Product thinking
Deciding what to build first, what to drop, which number should move, and arguing for it with product managers and engineers.
A case study that names the metric, the trade-off and what you would measure after launch.
1. Discovery
AI can sort and summarise notes. It cannot sit across from a nervous shop owner and notice what they did not say.
2. Interaction
First drafts of flows now take minutes. Choosing which flow is right for this business is still yours.
3. Visual
Generated screens look polished and generic. A taste that fits one brand is the part that sells.
4. System
Tools can propose components. Keeping a system consistent as a product grows is slow human work.
5. Product thinking
Not automated. This is the layer that separates a product designer from a screen maker.

Low. Most tools have free plans.
A live site a stranger can open.
Self-taught, portfolio-first, then freelance or small-team work
Scalable

You control the pace, a real project sells directly, and the work can grow into a niche practice or studio. Risk: Crowded at the bottom. Outside feedback is the missing piece for most self-taught people.
Another degree (engineering, BCA, commerce, arts) plus a design portfolio
Scalable with a business layer

Domain plus design is scarce, for example fintech or health plus product design. The business layer is consulting for that domain. Risk: Needs a visible switch story and a shipped project, not only a course.
B.Des from NID, or from IIT-level programmes through UCEED
Not so scalable

Rank-gated seats, many years before pay grows, and a degree alone does not skip the portfolio. Strong peer network is the real prize. Risk: Two competitions in a row. Keep a self-built skill and a second route alive while you prepare.
Short paid course or bootcamp only
Not so scalable

Many people finish the same practice projects, so the output looks alike. It scales only if the course forces a real, tested project. Risk: Paying for information that is already free (YouTube, Figma Learn, Nielsen Norman Group articles).
Private design diploma with no placement record
Not so scalable

Paid value should be feedback, a review standard and placement access. Ask for last year's real outcomes before paying. Risk: Spending more than about 10% of the education budget without course-specific proof.
Entry through web design or front-end work, then move toward product
Scalable with a business layer
Paid work can start earlier than in product teams. The business layer is a small studio or retainer clients. Risk: Template sites are the first thing AI builders squeeze.

Summarising interviews and feedback
Fast first pass. Check every quote against the recording.
Deciding which complaint is the real problem and which is noise.
Wireframes and screen variations
Figma Make turns a prompt into a working prototype or app, and press coverage reports a Figma and Anthropic feature that brings generated interface code back into Figma as editable design.
Fitting the flow to one business, one budget and one engineering team.
Resizing, format versions, clean-ups
The most exposed junior task. Fueler's hiring-data roundup lists these as the junior tasks most exposed to automation.
Little. Do not build a portfolio out of this work.
Design system upkeep
Tools help name and document. Quality is uneven.
Governing change across teams. Mid-level and senior openings ask for this.
Accessibility checks
Automated checkers catch contrast and labels.
Testing with people who rely on assistive tools and judging trade-offs.

High, but not India
You want a fast, safe, high-paying tech job in a few months
That is the story that sells courses. Junior openings are scarce and the first job often takes longer than the course did.
You enjoy drawing screens but dislike talking to customers or engineers
Layers 1 and 5 of the job are conversation. Pure visual work is the layer AI tools copy best.
You plan a large loan for a private diploma

Avoid education debt unless a credential is legally required. Design is not. Spend about 10% of the education budget on the course and keep the rest for tools, projects and living costs. Above roughly 20%, you need course-specific proof.
You cannot show unfinished work to strangers and take blunt feedback
The field runs on critique. Without it, a portfolio stays flat.
